scenes.title: How learning actually works
scenes.sub: Ranked techniques · illusions of skill · attention and learning
scenes.say: Chapter six. How learning actually works, and why so much of it is an illusion.
A recall from chapter five. What are the two ways background sound breaks your thinking?
scenes.sayA: Changing sound disrupts holding things in order, and understandable words compete with meaning. Rap hits both.
scenes.a: Changing sound breaks order; understandable words compete with meaning

scenes.text: A landmark review rated ten study techniques. *Practice testing* and *spaced practice*: high. ~Rereading, highlighting, summarising~: low.
scenes.note: The low ones are what most learners do
scenes.say: A landmark review rated ten study techniques. It rated practice testing and spaced practice as high utility, and rated rereading, highlighting and summarising as low, even though those are what most learners do.

scenes.head: Techniques ranked by evidence (effect sizes)
scenes.say: Later meta-analyses put numbers on the ranking. Spaced retrieval, testing yourself at intervals, beat cramming the same practice, with an effect of 0.74. Self-explanation came in at 0.55. Retrieval practice, producing from memory, at about 0.5, in the lab and in 222 classroom studies. Interleaving, mixing types instead of blocking them, at 0.42, though highly variable. And generation, producing the answer rather than reading it, at 0.4. Rereading and highlighting sit at the bottom.

scenes.head: Spacing: how far apart?
scenes.text: Best gap ≈ *20 to 40 percent* of how long you need to remember it, for a one-week horizon, falling to ~5 to 10 percent~ for a year.
scenes.note: Need it for a week? Review after a day or two.
scenes.say: How far apart should you space? For a one-week horizon, the best gap is about 20 to 40 percent of how long you need to remember it, falling to 5 to 10 percent for a whole year. So if you need something for a week, review it after a day or two.

scenes.head: Worked examples: the expertise reversal

items: Study complete expert scripts and edits
The same examples stop helping, and can hurt

scenes.say: Worked examples, meaning complete expert scripts and edits, give novices a large early benefit. But that benefit fades, and can reverse, as expertise grows. So study complete expert work early, then shift toward producing your own as you improve. And matching teaching to learning styles has no support: the few properly designed tests contradicted it.

scenes.head: For skills, retrieval means producing
scenes.text: Write a hook *without looking* at the reference. Rebuild a transition *with the tutorial closed*. Then ~compare~.
scenes.say: For skills rather than facts, retrieval means producing from memory. Write a hook without looking at the reference. Rebuild a transition with the tutorial closed. Then compare your version with the original.

scenes.head: Performance now vs learning that lasts
scenes.say: How smoothly learning goes is a poor guide to how much you learn. Conditions that boost what you can do right now, like cramming, blocking and rereading, differ from those that build durable learning, like spacing, interleaving, testing and generating. Learners even rated cramming as more effective than interleaving, after their own test scores showed the opposite.

scenes.head: Illusions of competence
items: A fluent, polished lecturer raised confidence, not scores
Active classes: students learned more, but felt they learned less
Traditional lectures: 1.5× more likely to fail
scenes.say: The evidence is consistent. A fluent, polished lecturer raised students' confidence but not their scores. Physics students learned more from active instruction but felt they learned less. And across 225 studies, active learning raised exam scores, with students in traditional lectures one and a half times more likely to fail.

scenes.head: Watching tutorials
scenes.text: Repeatedly watching someone perform a skill raised people's *belief* they could do it, ~without improving their actual ability~.
scenes.note: Only a brief hands-on attempt reduced the illusion
scenes.say: Most directly relevant to you: across 6 experiments with 2,225 people, repeatedly watching someone else perform a skill raised people's belief that they could do it, without improving their actual ability. Only a brief hands-on attempt reduced the illusion. The press release was titled: watching how-to videos on YouTube gives people a false sense of expertise.

scenes.head: AI: the same trap, built in
scenes.say: AI has the same trap built in. In a field experiment with about 1,000 high-school maths students, unrestricted GPT-4 raised practice performance by 48 percent. But once access was removed, those students scored 17 percent worse than students who never had it. A tutor version that gave hints instead of answers largely removed the harm.

scenes.head: Anthropic's trial: 52 engineers, quiz afterwards
scenes.say: In Anthropic's own trial with 52 engineers learning a new code library, the AI-assisted group averaged 50 percent on a follow-up quiz, against 67 percent for those who coded by hand. The engineers who kept their skills asked conceptual questions and fixed errors themselves, rather than handing over the work. And in a survey of 319 knowledge workers, more confidence in AI went with less critical thinking.

scenes.head: Learning design controls mind-wandering
scenes.say: Learning design also controls mind-wandering, which matters most for you. In a 21-minute video lecture, brief tests after each segment cut mind-wandering from about 40 percent to 19 percent, and raised final scores from 68 to 90 percent. Across 73 studies, mind-wandering in the moment predicted poorer reading comprehension, while a general tendency to daydream barely predicted anything. The way you set up a session can outweigh your daydreaming tendency.

scenes.text: Heavy short-form video use goes with *poorer attention* and ~weaker impulse control~ across 71 studies.
scenes.note: Correlation only. Unfinished tasks also leave ‘attention residue’.
scenes.say: Heavy short-form video use correlates with poorer attention and weaker impulse control across 71 studies, though which causes which is not established. And switching away from an unfinished task leaves attention residue that drags on the next one. Finishing a unit creates closure.

scenes.text: Watching, polish, fluency and AI answers all deliver the *feeling of progress*, which is ~exactly what a success fantasy delivers~.
scenes.say: Notice the common thread. Watching, polish, fluency and AI-generated answers all deliver the feeling of progress. That is exactly what a success fantasy delivers.
Which two techniques top the evidence ranking, and which popular ones sit at the bottom?
scenes.sayA: Testing yourself and spacing your practice are at the top. Rereading, highlighting and summarising are at the bottom.
scenes.a: Top: self-testing and spacing. Bottom: rereading, highlighting, summarising.

scenes.say: In the GPT-4 study, what happened once the AI was taken away, and what fixed it?
scenes.sayA: Students scored 17 percent worse than those who never had it. A tutor that gave hints instead of answers largely removed the harm.
scenes.a: 17% worse without it. Hint-only tutoring largely fixed it.
